EICMA 2026 • 2026 EICMA's Speed Legends Exhibit Was Not To Be Missed – See the Bikes That Paved MotoGP History
Ultra-Rare 1970 Hemi Superbird Never Raced NASCAR, Instead Father and Son Hit 220 MPH in It
26 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
This 1970 Plymouth Hemi Superbird was bought brand new by SCTA veteran Jim Lindsley to conquer the salt instead of NASCAR ovals. One of just 135 ever built, this car shattered the 220 mph barrier at Bonneville in 1975 to become the world’s fastest production car. Raced for 18 years by Jim and his son, the Superbird still retains its original, numbers-matching 426 Hemi engine today.
Back in 1970, Plymouth built the Superbird with a sole purpose: to dominate NASCAR’s high-banked superspeedways. Yet, one of the rarest examples ever to roll off the assembly line never turned a wheel on a paved oval in its life.
Instead, Southern California Timing Association veteran and co-founder of the Gear Grinders club Jim Lindsley purchased a brand-new, Alpine White Plymouth Hemi Superbird from the showroom floor and took it straight to the flats of El Mirage and Bonneville to make history. And history he made.
Right from the get-go, Jim Lindsley had zero intention of using it as a street car. All he wanted to do was see how fast Plymouth’s NASCAR aero warrior could go on salt. And in 1971, the car logged a one-way pass of 206 mph at Bonneville. This achievement made Jim and his son, Larry, the very first father-and-son duo inducted into the prestigious Bonneville 200 MPH Club.
Photo: Mecum Auctions To earn a shot at an official record, a car must first make a single run down the salt that beats the existing class record. So in 1972, the Lindsleys were back at Bonneville. Their Superbird ran 211.76 mph, successfully topping the existing 210.048 mph Class B Production record to qualify.
After proving its speed in 1972, the Lindsleys returned in 1973 and recorded the fastest overall speed in their specific competition category (Class B Production), earning the "First in Class" trophy for that event. And they didn't stop there.
During Speed Week in 1975, father and son broke the 220 mph (322 kph) barrier at Bonneville. That run officially made the 1970 Plymouth Hemi Superbird the fastest production car on Earth at the time, a record that stood for years.
However, the exact SCTA record breaker isn't publicly documented. The SCTA archives don’t pinpoint the exact driver or year that beat the Superbird's 1975 Class B Production mark, though it stood well into the 1980s before newer cars surpassed it.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Plymouth built roughly 1,935 Superbirds for NASCAR homologation in 1970, and only 135 left the factory with the 426 Hemi V8 engine like this car. Of the 135 Hemi-powered cars, only 77 were equipped with the automatic transmission like this one, which makes it extremely rare.
The Lindsleys raced the Superbird for its first two seasons using the factory Hemi, rated at 425 horsepower (431 metric horsepower) and 490 pound-feet (664 Newton meters) of torque. Plymouth did not publish an official factory top speed; road tests and gearing calculations with the standard 3.55:1 rear axle place stock top speed right around 144 mph (232 kph) at redline.
Every 426 Hemi Superbird with an auto box came standard with the A36 Performance Axle Package featuring a 3.55:1 Sure-Grip differential. While its aerodynamic body could exceed 200 mph in NASCAR trim, the factory street gearing capped its top speed below 150 mph (241 kph).
The father and the son eventually realized how rare their car was and were afraid they might ruin it. So, in order to push it to its limits, yet protect its rarity, they pulled the Hemi V8 out and placed it into climate-controlled storage.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Jim and his son, Larry, campaigned the 1970 Plymouth superbird at both El Mirage dry lake and the Bonneville Salt Flats from 1970 through 1988, running various race-prepped configurations for further record attempts.
The original 426 Hemi engine wasn’t reunited with the chassis until 2000, during the 1970 Plymouth Superbird’s first restoration. Now it features proper dual Carter AFB four-barrel carburetors and is mated to a correct 1970 Hemi-spec A727 TorqueFlite three-speed automatic transmission.
Because the Superbird ran in the SCTA Production classes, rules required the factory interior, including the original black dashboard, door panels, and trim, to remain intact. However, the chassis still wears physical evidence of engineering that took it to over 220 mph (322 kph).
For instance, the rear tail lamp panel retains the original access holes drilled for the stopping parachute cables. The passenger-side front fender still features holes from an experimental period fuel-cell installation used to balance front-end downforce at extreme speeds.
Photo: Mecum Auctions While the car wore several liveries across its 18-year racing career, it was refinished in 2021 to match its original 1970/1971 Bonneville race look. Today, looking just like it did over half a century ago, the 1970 Plymouth Superbird is scheduled to cross the auction block January 15, 2027, at Mecum’s Kissimmee event in Florida.
The record-breaking aero warrior is going with its original factory broadcast sheet, original pink slip title issued in Jim Lindsley’s name, a set of original Rallye wheels, and an extensive archive of period Bonnevile racing photographs.

This Murdered-Out Lamborghini Urus SE Looks Like a High-Riding Batmobile, Yours if You Want It
12 photos
Photo: Instagram | jesus.spec
Lamborghini may not care that much about the SE version of the Urus , because this model, just like the non-electrified S and Performante, not to mention the original pre-facelifted iteration, are dead and buried, and the sole-surviving Urus today is the SE Performante.
The latest iteration of the ultra popular (for an exotic) model was officially shown to the world earlier this year, and for whatever reason, it does not get that much attention. But that does not mean that it is a flop. Far from it, to be honest. It’s likely due to the fact that the Urus is not exactly a fresh model, even if the SE Performante is, because it has soldiered on with a few styling tweaks on the outside and some changes beneath the skin ever since 2017.
That is when the original Lamborghini Urus entered production at the Sant’Agata Bolognese factory in Italy, becoming the brand’s second most adventurous model ever after the LM002, aka the Rambo Lambo. And for what it’s worth, it was eventually joined by a third adventurous Raging Bull, namely the Huracan Sterrato , with its jacked-up design, and exclusive features inside and out and beneath the skin, which retired the brand’s previous-generation “baby” supercar.
Lamborghini’s new Urus SE Performante features a few stylistic tweaks on the outside, though they are discreet, so unless one is a fan or very familiar with this model, they might not be able to tell it apart from the demised variants. The most important upgrade lies beneath the skin, though, where the 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 plug-in hybrid powertrain has been massaged to produce 801 hp (597 kW/812 ps) and 738 lb-ft (1,000 Nm) of torque combined.
Photo: Instagram | jesus.spec This makes it 12 hp (9 kW /12 ps) punchier than the old Urus SE , and 144 hp (107 kW/146 ps) more powerful than the S and Performante. This represents a 160 hp (119 kW/162 ps) boost over the original Urus. The model has a 194 mph (312 kph) top speed, needs 3.3 seconds to zip to 62 mph (100 kph), identical to the demised Urus Performante, and has a 37-mile (60 km) range on zero emissions.
With this short Lamborghini Urus history lesson behind us, it is now time to put the spotlight on the pictured vehicle, which is a brand new Urus SE. This machine has obviously been visited by the tuning fairy, as it has a murdered-out design. It has a satin black look on the outside, with a few glossy black elements here and there. The reflectors on the sides of the front bumper haven’t been darkened out, but the windows have.
There is no detail about the wheels, suspension, and other elements in the short caption on social media post embedded at the bottom of the page, which only reveals the model year, mileage, and asking price. It is a 2026 Lamborghini Urus SE that has 858 miles (1,381 km) under its belt, and it costs... Actually, we will leave this information away for now, revealing it toward the end of the story.
On the inside, the plug-in hybrid exotic crossover features light brown leather upholstery on the seats, parts of the dashboard panel, and door cards, with some white stitching for contrast. The Raging Bull’s logo is embroidered into the headrests. The pillars and headliner appear to have been wrapped in Alcantara in a hue similar to the leather upholstery, and a panoramic roof is also on deck, alongside the three main screens, and other features.
Photo: Instagram | jesus.spec With zero mods, the Lamborghini Urus SE hits 62 mph (100 kph) in 3.4 seconds, one-tenth of a second slower than its SE Performante predecessor, and has an identical top speed. Its plug-in hybrid twin-turbo V8 develops 789 hp (589 kW/800 ps) and 701 pound-feet (950 Nm) of torque. And given that this example is still brand new, it is likely that no horses have escaped the stable just yet.
A used Lamborghini Urus SE will typically set you back between $270,000 and almost $400,000 in today’s used car market in the New World. Therefore, one must have really deep pockets if they with to own such a thing. A nearly model year with quite a few miles under its belt can sometimes end up costing close to the $250,000 mark, whereas new examples can change hands for over $350,000 and sometimes close to the $400,000 mark, depending on the options.
Now that you know how much one of these usually retails for in today’s used car market on our shores, how much do you think the 2026 Lamborghini Urus SE, with its 858 miles, costs? The answer is $339,995. The vehicle is advertised on social media (Instagram) by @jesus.spec, and you know what to do if you really want it, right? But would you really blow $340K on this thing? Provence Tiny House: Built for the Road and Styled for an Enchanting Ambiance
17 photos
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois
A tiny house named after the famous Provence region in France instantly brings to mind thoughts of idle days under the Mediterranean sun, uninterrupted comfort, and an everyday living experience that feels like an eternal vacation. “La Provencale” ticks all these boxes and much more, in a way that only a true French tiny house could.
It takes a special kind of person to appreciate artisan French tiny homes to the fullest, just like someone who prefers wooden sailing yachts instead of motor megayachts, or a vintage watch rather than a smart one. There’s something nostalgic and deeply comforting about a compact house on wheels made entirely out of wood, from the backbone to the interior wall paneling and exterior cladding.
Add to that touches of local French artistry and craftsmanship filled with the heritage of specific local regions, and you get a mobile house that is much than a practical alternative to conventional housing. A French tiny house looks like a blast from the past, yet timeless at the same time – a mysterious and wonderful time capsule that will feel just as welcoming and comforting decades from now on.
If there’s something that French tiny house artisans excel at, that’s building road-ready dwellings that are compact, lightweight, and easy transportable, while also furnished, equipped, and styled for long-term comfort that feels instantly familiar. There are many Nordic-style tiny homes out there, for instance, but they all have a similar “vacation home” vibe due to the extreme minimalism. French tiny homes are different, sometimes loud, often bold, and never dull.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois Tiny house Provencale proudly bears the name of one of the most popular and beloved French regions, synonymous with glorious landscapes, natural living, rich cultural heritage, and an overall “joie de vivre” (the joy of living). It embodies this richness through a warm, bohemian aesthetic that turns a compact interior into a peaceful cocoon.
This tiny home’s builder, the Occitania-based Mon Reve en Bois, has a generous portfolio of larger homes on wheels as well, similar to what would be called XL tiny homes in the US or certain parts of Europe. On the other hand, tiny house Provencale aims to offer the same signature style and functionality in a compact frame that is specifically intended for extensive travel and easy relocation.
With a length of just a little over six meters (21 feet), and a 2.5-meter width (8 feet), this compact house on wheels is the perfect travel companion. It’s a perfect choice for the modern nomad dreaming of extended vacations without sacrificing comfort, but it’s just as convenient for an owner who’s ready to downsize and experience tiny living full-time.
It’s the ingenious layout and beautiful styling that set this tiny home apart. As small and restrictive as it may seem, it’s actually meant to accommodate up to four people, with the addition of a fully-equipped bathroom and a versatile kitchen. All the basics for residential accommodation are covered, and there’s something else – a dedicated dining area with four seats becomes the unexpected perk that takes this tiny home from modest to elevated.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois Over time, French artisans have perfected the art of enhancing functionality even in the most compact tiny home interiors. It doesn’t always look flawless, but it certainly feels full of life, from the bespoke furniture and rustic kitchens to the quirky staircases and countryside-inspired décor. It’s not luxury, but it’s warmer and cozier than a regular cookie-cutter tiny house.
Considering its size, this tiny house offers remarkable flexibility. A two-bedroom configuration features a ground-level bedroom (with a unique and memorable design) and a loft right on top of it. Together, these two rooms can accommodate up to four people without having to sacrifice other living areas.
For better space efficiency, the kitchen was moved to one end of the house instead of the classic central placement. This makes room for a spacious dining area, a welcomed surprise for this type of compact layout, enhancing not just everyday living but also the joy of sharing meals with loved ones, friends and family. Tiny homes, especially the ones that focus primarily on radical downsizing, can lack the joy of togetherness, but the Tiny House from Provence is an exception.
The classic all-wood interior of French tiny homes is sweetened, in this case, with colorful pops of red evoking the Mediterranean warmth. These simple colorful accents are enough to brighten up the timber interior, while decorative plants and pieces of artwork further reinforce the Provence-inspired joyful ambiance. On the outside, this aesthetic is matched by the red-tile roof and plain timber cladding.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois The rustic-style timber shutters added to all the windows and even the main entrance are not just a style accent but an important factor for long-term comfort. They might seem odd in a world where indoor-outdoor design with massive glazing and almost full transparence is so prevalent, but they are authentic when it comes to the idyllic French countryside lifestyle. Comfort requires privacy, and deep rest needs a break from all stimuli.
With all shutters closed, this tiny house becomes a silent cocoon where one can truly rejuvenate through deep rest and a return to natural living. The ground-floor bedroom speaks of that also – it’s not your common Scandinavian-style open bedroom with a huge panoramic window and nothing to isolate it from the rest of the house. This is a dreamy, bohemian, and old-fashioned alcove bedroom that feels like a self-contained personal island inside the actual home.
Apart from the enchanting ambiance, there’s a very practical benefit for this type of alcove design. It’s much more compact than a Nordic-style open bedroom that would typically take up one end of the layout. Instead, this French tiny house fits the bathroom right next to this tiny alcove, underneath the loft. Even so, the bedroom is furnished with a comfy, two-person bed, and it even provides storage in the form of built-in drawers under the bed.
This entire fairytale boudoir is custom-crafted and therefore perfectly adjusted to the layout. The matching curtain is another charming detail that adds privacy, and there’s also a full-height closet for clothes and personal items in the small space between the bedroom and the dining area. A ladder provides access to the loft above this area, which, unlike a staircase, doesn’t require additional floor space –it’s the most efficient solution, although not the most comfortable.
Photo: Mon Reve en Bois The loft bedroom is big enough for two but highly rustic in terms of design – there are no expansive windows (only a tiny one in the back), no plush carpeting, and no built-in cabinetry. A minimalist, however, will appreciate the warmth of the timber all-around, as well as the refreshing simplicity.
Both the kitchen and the bathroom are equipped with all the essential appliances, and the kitchen features all bespoke cabinets and shelves. This particular placement didn’t allow for conventional cupboards, but the floating shelves above the countertop look even more charming. The dining table with four seats actually takes up very little floor space thanks to the ingenious location, and it can double as a workspace.
Despite its size and rustic design, this French tiny house looks as bright and airy as a much bigger home on wheels. The peaceful comfort it provides doesn’t make it dark or cramped, and this harmonious balance of natural light and residential-style comfort is what makes it so appealing.

Chevy’s Corvette E-Ray Convertible 3LZ Is Now a Five-Digit Affair in USA
13 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
Chevrolet may have pulled the plug on the E-Ray version of the C8-generation Corvette, replacing it with the Grand Sport X , but that does not make the first-ever electrified variant of the ‘Vette, as well as the first one to feature all-wheel drive, any less exciting.
In fact, these things are still worth a lot of money on the used car market, but if you know where to look and are patient enough, then you could land one for five digits. Mind you, it does not have to be a beaten-up example that has seen plenty of action over the years, because you could aim straight for an open-top 3LZ that is still brand new, and has had a single owner in the papers ever since it left the dealership.
Don’t believe us? Well, then you should know that the ‘Vette pictured in the gallery changed hands for $99,500. It is a 2025 model year Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray Convertible 3LZ , which was bought by the seller new back in March 2025. The man paid $136,890, as per the attached window sticker, and after putting only 570 miles (920 km) on the clock, he decided to let it go, stating that him and the missus are driving something bigger, and he does not have the time to enjoy the blue-collar electrified supercar.
Do you somehow think that this machine must have been involved in an accident, or that the mileage is not real? That’s not the case, because the Carfax history report reveals that the Arctic White paint finish has never touched or has been touched by another vehicle, nor something solid for that matter, and that the mileage is correct. This ride has a clean Iowa title, and before being sold, it was located in Clive, IA.
Photo: Cars&Bids There is no flaws category in the listing that we will link toward the end of the story, and if you must know, there are no modifications either. This 2025 Chevy Corvette E-Ray Convertible 3LZ features 20-inch wheels at the front and 21-inch wheels at the rear, which are backed up by the carbon ceramic brakes, and also benefits from the Magnetic Selective Ride Control, and the nose-lift system with memory function.
Other notable equipment mentioned in the ad includes the power-retractable hardtop, Adrenaline Red stitching, Torch Red seatbelts, and carbon fiber and sueded steering wheel. Suede is the material that dominates the cockpit, and there are several red inserts for contrast, as mentioned above, which also include the red 12 o’clock marker on the steering wheel. And the wall of buttons is also present, if you are into that sort of thing.
Care to talk about the firepower? Well, as you likely know, the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray came with a 6.2-liter V8, shared with the era’s Stingray (the latest model year has a 6.7L V8), and with the electric trickery up and running, it had 655 hp (489 kW/664 ps) and 595 pound-feet (807 Nm) of torque in total. The model took just 2.5 seconds to reach 60 mph (97 kph), and that’s almost as fast as the Lamborghini Revuelto, which costs a lot more.
Due to the low mileage, the pictured Chevy Corvette E-Ray has not required any servicing yet, the seller noted. Besides the car, the new owner will also get the window sticker, as well as the usual manuals, two key fobs, a trickle charger, and a serialized crystal glass model.
Photo: Cars&Bids Nationwide listings for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray usually span from over $85,000 to more than $120,000 in today’s used car market, and the value depends on the trim level (1LZ, 2LZ, or 3LZ), as well as the body style, mileage, and overall appearance. Brand new examples with a single owner in the papers since new do not tend to fall into the five-digit category, but as we already told you above, this one did.
So, congratulations to the new owner for landing a great machine that was almost $137,000 new some one and a half years ago. This ride depreciated $37,390, and it ended up costing the seller a whopping $65+ per mile. A chauffeured limo service would have been more than ten times more affordable. It is worth noting that the title will become available only after the loan has been paid off, and the sale proceeds will be used to satisfy it.
This particular 2025 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray Convertible 3LZ changed hands recently as part of an online auction that ended on November 12, 2026. It was advertised on Cars&Bids, and if you want to find out more about it, and check it out in additional pictures, then you should access the listing here . However, before you do that, let us know if you would have paid $99,500 for it, given that it is a brand new example with zero issues.

Quirky Subaru SVX Grand Tourer Comes Back to Virtual Life Based on the Subaru Sport Mobility Concept
10 photos
Photo: Theottle / YouTube
The Japanese automaker Subaru is extremely beloved in places like North America, especially the United States. As such, we weren’t surprised to see the local division recovering from the slump from earlier this year.
The folks over from Subaru are slowly but steadily coming back to positive results – October 2026 saw a six percent increase across the US automotive market to 54k units, with sales led by Crosstrek and Forester going up by 26% both during the month. Even the WRX is up by 55% year-to-date, but Subaru of America needs a continued punch to come out of the woods: year-to-date total deliveries are now almost 530k units, down close to one percent from last year.
You can’t say they’re not taking measures. For example, the 2027 Subaru Outback has become more affordable than last year, starting at $32,995 MSRP instead of almost $35k, thanks to the new model year bringing with it a fresh entry-level model. Additionally, we heard that Subie made an in-house EV packing 510 hp and featuring Aisin drive units plus Panasonic battery cells, skipping the usual cooperation with Toyota.
However, a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators has stopped dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI because they have a fresh proposal: this virtual artist, better known as " Theottle " on social media, has resorted to CGI slicing and dicing an older concept to make a fresh Subaru GT coupe for the lineup.
It makes sense: Subaru only sells the Impreza compact five-door hatchback, BRZ RWD entry-level sports car, and the WRX compact sports sedan in America, so a range-topping passenger car might also fit in for the right price and with the right characteristics.
His proposal is quite simple: bring back the quirky Subaru SVX nameplate, a two-door grand tourer with four-wheel drive produced from 199 through 1996 with a 3.3-liter boxer-six engine. This pixel master’s vision includes the defunct Audi A5 coupe as the placeholder for the unofficial, hypothetical SVX design project in his latest behind-the-scenes making-of video, and for the styling he used the cool Subaru Sport Mobility Concept all-electric sports coupe presented at the 2023 Japan Mobility Show.
The model was Subie’s vision for all-electric performance at the time, and he remembered it and now set out to imagine its production-ready version as a next-generation Subaru SVX. Naturally, the CGI expert didn’t forget about “SVX’s most distinctive design cue: its signature window-within-a-window glass design.”
So, what do you think – yay or nay? Should they make something like this and risk a potential failure in the US, where EVs aren’t beloved at the moment, or hope that if they fit it with that new EV powertrain, it will turn into a worthy successor to Subaru’s iconic 1990s grand touring coupe?

EICMA 2026 • Benelli Showed the World Its New Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept at EICMA 2026 and It's a Triple!
Third-Gen 2028 Ford GT Virtually Decides to Quarrel With the All-New Ferrari 849 Testarossa HEV Star
17 photos
Photo: tedoradze.giorgi / Instagram
The story of the Ford GT mid-engine two-seater sports car is deeply inspired by the ‘rags-to-riches’ legend of the Ford GT40 racing car that competed during the 1960s in European endurance racing and the World Sportscar Championship.
Its prime focus was beating Scuderia Ferrari, hence the automotive version of the ‘rags-to-riches’ legend, as Ford decided to put an end to the reign of the Prancing Horse at the ultra-prestigious 24 Hours of Le Mans race, won by the Italians for six years in a row from 1960 to 1965. The rules of the time asked for road cars to be made for homologation purposes, and the Ford GT40 thus also reached the streets – albeit in very small batches.
Years later, Ford wanted to rekindle the stunning success story and created the first-generation Ford GT, a direct homage to the historically significant GT40, a consecutive four-time winner of the 24 Hours of Le Mans (1966–1969), which also included the iconic 1-2-3 finish in 1966. The original Ford GT was a clear retro-modern supercar that brought the GT40 into the modern era – fueled by a 5.4-liter supercharged Ford Modular V8 heart.
Production was limited for the 2025 and 2006 model years , with a mere 4k units produced, and the nameplate went on hiatus until the 2015 North American International Auto Show when the Blue Oval presented the second-gen Ford GT as a 2017 model year. Again, production was even more exotic: 1,350 units were made until 2022, and then another pause.
We’re in 2026, but still there’s no word about a third-generation Ford GT, with the Blue Oval instead preoccupied with its official return to Formula 1 with Red Bull Racing and via Red Bull Ford Powertrains as a technical partner while it’s also developing an in-house Le Mans Hypercar with a 5.4-liter V8 engine for the 2027 World Endurance Championship.
No worries, as the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI have taken the task upon themselves. More precisely, Giorgi Tedoradze, the Georgia-based industrial designer better known as " tedoradze.giorgi " on social media, has a stylish third-generation Ford GT in his CGI-loving mind for the 2028 model year and showed it as their latest unofficial, hypothetical design project dwelling on a racetrack alongside its illustrious predecessor.
If that wasn’t enough, the mid-engine supercar, painted in white and featuring classic Ford Racing blue stripes, also appeared next to the potential prime rival – the 2026 Ferrari 849 Testarossa . As such, we can imagine the virtual artist has in mind a likewise PHEV setup with a V8 at its core. The Prancing Horse uses a 4.0-liter F154 FC twin-turbocharged V8 aided by electric motors and packs no less than 1,036 hp combined. source_document.body:
Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”
And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
What Tesla is selling
Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”
The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”
The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”
Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.
“Supported service areas” means Texas and Florida
Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.
And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.
Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.
Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential . NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.
Electrek’s Take
I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.
Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.
Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).
View all comments
And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027 , while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.
If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?
Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.
